question: We're playing best of five games to 11. In the third game, when do we switch ends?

answer.reasoning: The question describes a best-of-five match to 11 points and asks when ends are changed in the third game. Two sources bear on this: the standard Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2) (in force 2025-04-26), Law 8.1.3, which says players change ends in the third game when a side first scores 11 points (except in Handicap Matches); and the Alternative Laws of Badminton 2.0, format best-of-5-games-11 (in force 2027-01-04), Clause 8.1.3, which is the alternative to that law and instead says players change ends at the end of the third game if there is to be a fourth game — i.e., under that format there is no mid-game change of ends in the third game. The ITTO 5.6.10 clause also describes the umpire's procedure in a third game after the rally that first takes a side to 11 points under the standard laws. Per the instructions, the standard rule is given first, then the alternative format with its in-force date.
answer.answer: Under the standard Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2) (in force 2025-04-26), Law 8.1.3: players change ends "in the third game when a side first scores 11 points, except in Handicap Matches (BWF Statute Section 4.1.3)". The Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5) (in force 2025-04-26), Clause 5.6.10, describe the corresponding procedure: in a third game, after the rally which first takes a side to 11 points, the Umpire calls the score followed immediately by "interval, change ends". However, for the exact format you describe — best of five games to 11 — the Alternative Laws of Badminton 2.0, format best-of-5-games-11 (in force 2027-01-04), Clause 8.1.3 differs: players change ends "at the end of the third game, if there is to be a fourth game;". So under that alternative format there is no change of ends during the third game itself; the change happens only at the end of the third game, and only if a fourth game is to be played.

question: My opponent shouted 'fault!' while I was playing my shot. What's the ruling?

answer.reasoning: The question asks about an opponent shouting 'fault!' during the user's stroke. Two sources bear directly: Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2) clause 13.4.5 makes it a fault if, in play, a player 'deliberately distracts an opponent by any action such as shouting or making gestures', and Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5) clause 5.9.1.4 specifies that 'A player calling 'fault', etc. to the opponent when making a stroke or after the opponent has made a stroke, shall be considered a deliberate distraction (Law 13.4.5)'. The user's scenario (opponent shouting 'fault!' while the user plays their shot) matches 5.9.1.4 exactly. The contrary nuance in itto-5.9.1.3 (shouting to a partner is not necessarily deliberate distraction) does not apply because the shout was directed at the opponent. Law 7.3 gives the consequence: the side winning a rally adds a point, and a side wins a rally if the opposing side commits a fault. Together these fully answer the question.
answer.answer: It is a fault by your opponent. Calling 'fault' (or similar) to the opponent while making a stroke or after the opponent has made a stroke is considered a deliberate distraction, which is a fault under Law 13.4.5 of the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26: 'deliberately distracts an opponent by any action such as shouting or making gestures'. As a result, your side wins the rally and adds a point to your score (Law 7.3: 'A side shall win a rally, if the opposing side commits a 'fault''). Note the distinction in the Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5): shouting to your own partner who is about to hit the shuttle is not necessarily deliberate distraction — but shouting 'fault!' at the opponent, as here, is.

question: When do we replay a rally? List every situation that counts as a let.

answer.reasoning: The question asks for the replay rule and the complete list of let situations. The relevant source is Law 14 of the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26: Law 14.1 says who calls a let, Law 14.3 says what happens when a let occurs (replay from the last service), and Law 14.2 with its subclauses 14.2.1–14.2.7 and 14.2.3.1–14.2.3.2 gives the exhaustive 'It shall be a let, if:' list. Together these answer the question fully, so no refusal is needed.
answer.answer: A rally is replayed when a ‘let’ is called. Under the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, ‘Let’ is called by the umpire, or by a player if there is no umpire, to halt play, and when a ‘let’ occurs, play since the last service shall not count and the player who served last shall serve again. Law 14.2 lists every situation that is a ‘let’: (1) the server serves before the receiver is ready (Law 9.4); (2) during service, the receiver and the server are both faulted; (3) after the service is returned, the shuttle is caught on the net and remains suspended on its top, or after passing over the net is caught in the net; (4) during play, the shuttle disintegrates and the base completely separates from the rest of the shuttle; (5) in the opinion of the umpire, play is disrupted or a player of the opposing side is distracted by a coach; (6) a line judge is unsighted and the umpire or Instant Review System is unable to make a decision; or (7) any unforeseen or accidental situation has occurred.

question: My partner cut his hand mid-game and it's bleeding. How long can we stop, and who can come on court to help?

answer.reasoning: The question has two parts: (1) how long play can stop for a bleeding injury, and (2) who may come on court to help. The Instructions to Technical Officials (ITTO 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26) directly cover both: clause 5.14.2 covers delay for a blood-flowing injury, clauses 3.6.1.1–3.6.1.4 and 3.6.1.6 cover who goes on court and for how long, and clause 5.14.1 covers the Umpire's role. The Laws of Badminton (5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26) add the general limit in Law 16.4.1 that play may not be delayed to recover wind or receive advice. No source gives a fixed number of minutes; the sources say 'well within a few minutes' and that the Umpire times the delay. Together the sources answer both parts, so no refusal is needed.
answer.answer: How long: For a blood-flowing injury, the game is delayed until the bleeding stops, the wound is suitably dressed, or the Referee advises the Umpire otherwise — there is no fixed number of minutes in the sources. The Referee must resolve the injury situation 'as quickly as possible and well within a few minutes so that play can be resumed or abandoned', and the Umpire times the delay caused by the injury. The Tournament Doctor may apply quick relief such as a bandage on a bleeding injury, but no time-consuming treatment is allowed on court except in the regular intervals, and then only if the Doctor estimates it can be completed (or nearly so) before the interval ends. Note the general limit in Law 16.4.1: 'Under no circumstances shall play be delayed to enable a player to recover strength or wind or to receive advice.' If the injury is severe and there is no doubt the player cannot continue, the regular process is disregarded and the Tournament Doctor gives first aid until the player can be transported to hospital. Who may come on court: When the Umpire calls in case of injury, the Referee and the Tournament Doctor shall immediately go on court. The Referee may allow a maximum of two persons on court to assist and advise the injured player and help with translation, and in fairness the opposing side must be allowed the same consideration. The Referee decides whether the Tournament Doctor or anyone else is required on court.

question: Water started dripping from the roof onto our court mid-game. What happens to the match and the score?

answer.reasoning: The question asks what happens to a match and score when water drips onto the court mid-game. The relevant sources are Law 16.3 (Suspension of play) in the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, and clauses 5.11.2–5.11.5 of the Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, which cover delays and suspension when playing conditions are affected. Together they answer both parts: the match is suspended (not a let, no rally replay), and the existing score stands. No source addresses water specifically, but the clauses cover circumstances affecting playing conditions and courts temporarily not playable, which is what dripping water is.
answer.answer: Water dripping onto the court is a circumstance affecting playing conditions that is not within the players' control, so play is suspended — it is not a 'let' and the rally is not replayed. Under Law 16.3.1 of the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2) (in force 2025-04-26), 'When necessitated by circumstances not within the control of the players, the umpire may suspend play for such a period as the umpire may consider necessary.' The Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5) (in force 2025-04-26) add that 'Play may be suspended by the Referee or Umpire if warranted by a circumstance affecting playing conditions' (Clause 5.11.2), and that if 'a court or its immediate surroundings needs repair, or it is temporarily not playable, the Umpire shall call the Referee (or the Referee shall go onto the court) and play be suspended until the court and its immediate surroundings are again suitable for play' (Clause 5.11.3). On the score: under Law 16.3.3, 'If play is suspended, the existing score shall stand and play shall be resumed from that point' — so the score at the moment of suspension is kept and the match continues from that point, with no point awarded or replayed for the interrupted rally. Procedurally, when play is suspended the Umpire calls 'Play is suspended' and notes 'S' on the scoring device or score-sheet (ITTO Clause 5.11.4); when play resumes, the Umpire notes the duration of the suspension, ensures the players are on the correct side of the net and in the correct service courts, then calls 'Are you ready?' followed by the score and 'Play' (ITTO Clause 5.11.5).

citations.quote: When necessitated by circumstances not within the control of the players, the umpire may suspend play for such a period as the umpire may consider necessary.
If play is suspended, the existing score shall stand and play shall be resumed from that point.

If, during a match, a court or its immediate surroundings needs repair, or it is temporarily not playable, the Umpire shall call the Referee (or the Referee shall go onto the court) and play be suspended until the court and its immediate surroundings are again suitable for play.
When play is suspended, the Umpire shall call: “Play is suspended” and note “S” on the scoring device or score-sheet, if used.

When play resumes after the suspension, the Umpire shall note the duration of the suspension and ensure that the players are on the correct side of the net and in the correct service courts, then call “Are you ready?” followed by the score and “Play”.

question: My opponent keeps flicking sweat onto the court. What can the umpire do about it?

answer.reasoning: The question asks what the umpire can do when a player flicking sweat contaminates the court. ITTO clause 5.9.1.6 directly covers this: a player throwing sweat or otherwise contaminating the court shall be reminded the conduct is unacceptable, with Law 16.7 applied if necessary. Laws 16.7.1.1–16.7.1.3 then set out the escalation (warning, then fault if previously warned, or fault for flagrant offence), and 16.7.2 adds that a faulted side is reported to the Referee, who may disqualify. ITTO 5.17.3 describes how a warning is administered (yellow card). Together these fully answer the question; no further search is needed.
answer.answer: The umpire should first remind the player that throwing sweat / contaminating the court and its immediate surroundings is unacceptable, and apply Law 16.7 if necessary (Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, clause 5.9.1.6). Under Law 16.7.1 (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26), the umpire administers the breach by: issuing a warning to the offending side (16.7.1.1); faulting the offending side if previously warned (16.7.1.2); or faulting the offending side in cases of flagrant offence or breach (16.7.1.3). When issuing a warning, the umpire calls the offending player over and calls "warning for misconduct" with a specific explanation, raising a yellow card above the head (ITTO 5.17.3). If a side is faulted, the umpire reports the offending side immediately to the Referee, who has the power to disqualify the offending side from the match (Law 16.7.2). question: The line judge couldn't see whether the shuttle landed in. What happens to the rally?

answer.reasoning: The question asks what happens to the rally when the line judge could not see the shuttle's landing. The sources cover this directly: Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2) Law 14.2.6 makes it a 'let' when a line judge is unsighted and the umpire or Instant Review System cannot make a decision; Law 17.6.6 says the umpire carries out the unsighted official's duties or plays a let; ITTO 7.0 (5) clause 2.5 says the umpire makes the decision when another official is unsighted, and a let is called when no decision can be made unless IRS is in use; ITTO 8.5/8.8 describe the line judge's unsighted signal. Together these fully answer the question, so no refusal is needed.
answer.answer: If the line judge could not see whether the shuttle landed in, the line judge signals 'unsighted' immediately by putting both hands up to cover the eyes (Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, clause 8.5; the approved hand signal is 'UNSIGHTED', clause 8.8). The umpire then makes the decision on the line call (ITTO 7.0 (5), clause 2.5: 'When another official is unsighted, the Umpire shall make the decision.'). If the umpire (or the Instant Review System, when in use) is unable to make a decision, the rally does not get a point either way — it shall be a 'let' and is replayed (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Law 14.2.6: 'It shall be a 'let', if: a line judge is unsighted and the umpire or Instant Review System is unable to make a decision'; see also Law 17.6.6: 'where an appointed official is unsighted, carry out that official's duties or play a 'let''; and ITTO 7.0 (5), clause 2.5: 'When no decision can be made, a 'let' shall be called (Law 17.6.6), unless IRS is in use, in which case it will be used to decide on the line call').

question: Can my coach get up from his chair and stand at the side of the court during the match?

answer.reasoning: The question asks whether a coach may stand at the side of the court during a match. The Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), Clause 5.12.2 ('Coaching from Off Court') directly answers this: coaches must be seated in their designated seats and must not stand court-side during the match except during the permitted intervals under Law 16.2. Reading Law 16.2 (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2)) gives the permitted intervals: Law 16.2.1 (not exceeding 60 seconds when the leading score reaches 11 in each game) and Law 16.2.2 (not exceeding 120 seconds between games). Together these fully answer the question, so no refusal is needed.
answer.answer: No. Under the Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 5.12.2, coaches must be seated in their designated seats and must not stand court-side during the match, except during the permitted intervals (Law 16.2). Those permitted intervals, per the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, are: not exceeding 60 seconds during each game when the leading score reaches 11 points (Law 16.2.1), and not exceeding 120 seconds between the first and second game and between the second and third game (Law 16.2.2). So your coach may get up and stand at the side of the court only during those intervals, not while play is ongoing.

question: What weight range is allowed for a plastic shuttle, and since our hall gets really hot and stuffy in summer, can we use a special type made for hot weather?

answer.reasoning: The question has two parts: (1) the allowed weight of a plastic (non-feathered/synthetic) shuttle, and (2) whether a special shuttle can be used in hot/stuffy conditions. Laws 2.2.6 and 2.3.3 answer the weight part: the standard shuttle weighs 4.74–5.50 g, and a non-feathered (synthetic/plastic) shuttle may vary up to 10 per cent from that because of the different specific gravity of synthetic materials. Law 2.4 answers the hot-weather part: modifications to the specifications are allowed, with the approval of the Member Association concerned, where atmospheric conditions due to altitude or climate make the standard shuttle unsuitable — but only subject to no variation in general design, speed and flight. Law 2.1 confirms shuttles may be made of synthetic materials with flight characteristics similar to a feathered shuttle. ITTO 3.5.4.7 additionally notes shuttles may need retesting when temperature/humidity change substantially, but that is about testing speed, not a special hot-weather shuttle type. No source describes a distinct 'hot weather' shuttle product; the only mechanism is Law 2.4.
answer.answer: Weight: the shuttle shall weigh from 4.74 to 5.50 grams (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Law 2.2.6). For a plastic (non-feathered) shuttle, measurements and weight are as in Laws 2.2.2, 2.2.3 and 2.2.6, but because of the difference in specific gravity and other properties of synthetic materials compared with feathers, a variation of up to 10 per cent is acceptable (Law 2.3.3) — i.e. roughly 4.27 g to 6.05 g. Hot weather: there is no separate 'hot weather shuttle' type in the Laws. However, Law 2.4 allows modifications to the specifications, subject to there being no variation in the general design, speed and flight of the shuttle, with the approval of the Member Association concerned, in places where atmospheric conditions due to either altitude or climate make the standard shuttle unsuitable. So in a hot, stuffy hall you may use a modified shuttle only with your Member Association's approval and only if its design, speed and flight are unchanged. Separately, the Referee may have shuttles retested if playing conditions such as temperature and humidity change substantially (ITTO 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 3.5.4.7), and the Referee is the sole judge of shuttle speed (ITTO Clause 5.13.3).

question: My opponent got a yellow card for swearing during the warm-up, before the umpire called 'Play'. Does it cost him a point now, and does the card go on his record after the tournament?

answer.reasoning: The question has two parts: (1) whether a yellow card for misconduct before 'Play' costs a point now, and (2) whether the card stays on the player's record after the tournament. ITTO 5.17.10 directly covers misconduct before the match on the Field of Play before 'Play' is called: the card has no effect on the score but counts if further offences occur during the match (Law 16.7.1.2). Law 16.7.1.2 says a previously warned side is faulted, and Law 7.3 says a fault means the opposing side wins the rally and adds a point — so a point is only at stake if he reoffends. For the record: ITTO 5.17.2 requires the umpire to record and report any misconduct to the Referee, and ITTO 3.7.3 requires the Referee to send BWF (or CC) a report on yellow and red cards after the tournament that may trigger further sanctions. ITTO 5.17.3 confirms the yellow card is the warning procedure under Law 16.7.1.1. All parts are answered by the sources.
answer.answer: No, the yellow card does not cost him a point now. Misconduct before the match while on the Field of Play before 'Play' has been called is administered as a warning (yellow card, Law 16.7.1.1), and per Instructions to Technical Officials 5.17.10, 'Any card(s) given shall have no effect on the score of the match but a card(s) shall be taken into account if further offences occur during the match (Law 16.7.1.2).' If he commits a further offence during the match, the offending side is then faulted under Law 16.7.1.2 ('faulting the offending side, if previously warned'), and a fault means the opposing side wins the rally and adds a point to its score (Law 7.3: 'A side shall win a rally, if the opposing side commits a ‘fault’'). So a point is only lost if he reoffends after the warning. As for the record: yes, the card is recorded and reported after the tournament. The umpire must 'Record and report to the Referee any incident of misconduct and the action taken' (ITTO 5.17.2), and 'The Referee shall immediately after the tournament send to BWF (or CC) a report on withdrawals, yellow and red cards, that may trigger further sanctions' (ITTO 3.7.3).
